'''''Melaleuca ericifolia''''', commonly known as '''swamp paperbark''', is a plant in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Myrtaceae]] and the genus ''[[Melaleuca]]'', native to south-eastern [[Australia]]. It is a rather variable species and some specimens resemble ''[[Melaleuca armillaris]]'' but its papery bark and smaller, more prolific flower heads distinguish it from that species. It often grows in swampy areas and the draining and clearing of these has reduced the numbers of the species, especially around [[Port Philip Bay]] near [[Melbourne]]. It is also similar to ''[[Melaleuca pustulata]]'', a [[Tasmania]]n endemic, but that species only grows in dry [[heath]].

==Description==
''Melaleuca ericifolia'' is a tall, dense shrub, sometimes a tree growing to a height of {{convert|9|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} with pale white or brownish papery bark. Its leaves are arranged alternately, sometimes in [[whorl (botany)|whorls]] of three. The leaves are dark green, linear in shape, {{convert|5-18|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.5-1.7|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas: their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|location=Canberra|isbn=978-1-922137-51-7|pages=154–155}}</ref><ref name=Holliday>{{cite book|last1=Holliday|first1=Ivan|title=Melaleucas: a field and garden guide|date=2004|publisher=Reed New Holland Publishers|location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W.|isbn=1-876334-98-3|pages=102–103|edition=2nd}}</ref><ref name=Costermans>{{cite book|author=Costermans, L.| title=Native Trees and Shrubs of South-eastern Australia |publisher=Rigby|location=Australia | year=1981 | isbn=0-7270-1403-X}}</ref><ref name=plantnet>{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Peter G.|title=''Melaleuca ericifolia''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Melaleuca~ericifolia|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney: Plantnet|access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref><ref name=Yarra>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca ericifloia''|url=http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/Residents/Trees_Vegetation/Yarra_Ranges_Plant_Directory/Yarra_Ranges_Local_Plant_Directory/Middle_Storey/Trees_3-25m/Melaleuca_ericifolia | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190911220634/http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au:80/Residents/Trees_Vegetation/Yarra_Ranges_Plant_Directory/Yarra_Ranges_Local_Plant_Directory/Middle_Storey/Trees_3-25m/Melaleuca_ericifolia |archive-date=2019-09-11 |publisher=Yarra Ranges Shire Council|access-date=25 January 2018}}</ref>

The flowers are creamy-white in colour, arranged in heads or spikes on the ends of branches which continue to grow after flowering. The spikes are up to {{convert|20|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter and {{convert|25|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and contain 10 to 40 individual flowers. The petals are {{convert|1.2-2.2|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flowers age. The stamens are arranged in five bundles around the flower, each bundle containing 7 to 14 stamens. Flowers appear from October to November in the species' native range and are followed by fruit which are woody [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]] {{convert|2.5-3.6|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3-5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} diameter, arranged in oblong cylinders along the stems.<ref name=Brophy/><ref name=Holliday/><ref name=Costermans/><ref name=plantnet/>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Melaleuca ericifolia'' was first formally described by English botanist [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in 1797 in ''[[Transactions of the Linnean Society of London]]''.<ref name=APNI(1)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca ericifolia''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/511362|publisher=APNI|access-date=24 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=Smith>{{cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=James Edward|title=Botanical Characters of Some Plants of the Natural Order of Myrti.|journal=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London|date=1797|volume=3|page=276|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13713#page/303/mode/1up|access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref> The variety ''Melaleuca ericifolia'' var. ''erubescens'' which was described by botanist [[George Bentham]] in ''[[Flora Australiensis]]''  in 1867 is currently regarded as a synonym of ''[[Melaleuca diosmatifolia]]''.<ref name=APNI(2)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca ericifolia'' var. ''erubescens'' Benth.|url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/511396|publisher=APNI|access-date=25 January 2018}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''ericifolia'') is a reference to the apparent similarity of the leaves of this species to those of ''[[Erica (plant)|Erica]]'' in the family [[Ericaceae]].<ref name="Brophy" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Swamp paperbark occurs in near-coastal areas of New South Wales south of [[Port Macquarie]]<ref name=plantnet/> to Port Philip Bay in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]]. It is also found on the islands of [[Bass Strait]]<ref name=Brophy/> and is common near the coast in the north, north east and west of Tasmania.<ref name=utas>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca ericifolia''|url=http://www.utas.edu.au/dicotkey/dicotkey/MYRTS/sMelaleuca_ercicifolia.htm|publisher=University of Tasmania|access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref> It grows beside streams and in coastal swamps in heath and dry sclerophyll forest.<ref name=Brophy/> Draining of swamps and land clearance have significantly reduced the numbers of this species in Victoria.<ref name=Holliday/><ref name=depi>{{cite web|title=Swamp paperbark|url=http://vro.depi.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/water_sss_swamp_paperbark|publisher=Victorian government department of environment and primary industries|access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref>

==Ecology==
This melaleuca has fragrant flowers which attract birds.<ref name=Greig>{{cite book|author=Greig, D.| title=The Australian Gardener's Wildflower Catalogue| publisher=Angus & Robertson|location= Australia | year=1987 | isbn=0-207-15460-0}}</ref> It is a clonal species and efforts have been made to use this characteristic to increase the efficiency of rehabilitating swampy areas with this species.<ref name=thesis>{{cite web|last1=Robinson|first1=Randall|title=PhD thesis: Regeneration mechanisms in Swamp Paperbark (''Melaleuca ericifolia'' Sm.) and their implications for wetland rehabilitation|url=http://vuir.vu.edu.au/1469/1/robinson.pdf|publisher=Victoria University, St.Albans, Victoria|access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Traditional use ===
Aboriginal people used the bark of this tree for paintings, blankets, and roofing for shelters. The wood was used for spears, clubs and digging sticks. Oil from the leaves was used for medicine and nectar from the flowers was used to make sweet drinks.<ref name=Yarra/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Scott |first1=Rob |last2=Blake |first2=Neil |last3=Campbell |first3=Jeannie |last4=Evans |first4=Doug |last5=Williams |first5=Nicholas |title=Indigenous Plants of the Sandbelt A Gardening Guide for South-eastern Melbourne. |date=2002 |publisher=Gardners Books |location=St Kilda |isbn=0-9581009-0-X |page=128}}</ref>

===Horticulture===
This species is a very hardy, fast-growing screen plant.<ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=ill. by Murray|title=Australian native plants: a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0-00-216575-9|page=263|edition=2}}</ref> It is able to withstand permanently wet soil, salt, coastal exposure, shade and moderate frost.<ref name=Greig/> Plants may be pruned to maintain them at a more compact size.<ref name=Greig/>

===Essential oils===
''Melaleuca ericifolia'' leaves have been analysed for their oil content and found to contain mostly 1,8-cineole ([[Eucalyptol]]) but also significant amounts of [[alpha-Pinene|α-pinene]].<ref name=Brophy/> The aromatic oil in the leaves has been used for dental and medical preparations and in scented soaps.<ref name=depi/>

===Other uses===
The foliage of this species has been used for brushwood [[Fence|fencing]]<ref name=depi/> and in [[Aviary|aviaries]] for nesting sites for species such as [[finch]]es.<ref name=Brophy/>
